question: A bell is struck with a felt beater, then with a steel hammer of the same mass moving at the same speed. Compared with the felt strike, what does the steel strike change about the sound?

answers.answer: The amplitude, and the mixture of the bell's own modes it excites — but not the frequency of any mode.
answers.feedback: Right. A kick sets a velocity and nothing else, so the motion afterwards is free decay: it rings at omega_d, which belongs to the bell. A harder, shorter strike delivers a larger impulse and its spectrum is flatter, so it feeds the higher modes more strongly — brighter, louder, same pitches.

answers.answer: The frequency of the ringing, because a stiffer impact drives the bell faster.
answers.feedback: The impact drives nothing after it is over, and it is over almost immediately. Once the hammer has left, the equation of motion has no force term at all, so the bell solves its own free-decay problem at its own omega_d. Nothing about the mallet appears in that frequency.

answers.answer: The decay rate, because a harder strike puts in more energy and takes longer to dissipate.
answers.feedback: Decay is exponential, so the time to fall by a given *factor* does not depend on where it started: gamma/2 is a property of the bell. A harder strike is louder for longer only in the sense that it starts higher up the same exponential.

answers.answer: Nothing measurable — the impulse response is a fixed property of the bell.
answers.feedback: G(t) is fixed, but the response is G scaled by the impulse J, so amplitude certainly changes. The invariant claim is narrower and more interesting: the *shape* in time is always the same, and only its size is yours to choose.

question: An oscillator with Q = 10 is kicked twice with equal impulses, the second kick landing exactly half a period after the first. What does the ringing look like afterwards?

answers.answer: Almost cancelled, at about 15% of a single kick — but not exactly zero.
answers.feedback: Right. Half a period puts the two contributions in antiphase, so they subtract, and the amplitude ratio is 1 - e^(-pi/2Q) = 0.15 at Q = 10. It is not zero because the first kick's ringing has already decayed a little by the time the second arrives, so the two amplitudes being subtracted are not equal.

answers.answer: Exactly cancelled — the two contributions are in antiphase and destroy each other completely.
answers.feedback: They are in antiphase, but cancellation also needs equal amplitudes, and damping has shrunk the first one by e^(-pi/2Q) before the second arrives. Exact cancellation would require Q to be infinite, which is the undamped oscillator that never settles.

answers.answer: Doubled — two kicks put in twice the impulse, so the response is twice as large.
answers.feedback: Impulses add, but responses add *as signed functions of time*, and here the second arrives when the first contribution is moving the other way. Doubling is what you get from kicks spaced a whole period apart, and even then only 1 + e^(-pi/Q) = 1.73 times, not 2.

answers.answer: Unchanged — the second kick arrives when the mass is at its turning point and does no work.
answers.feedback: A kick changes the velocity regardless of where the mass happens to be, so it always alters the motion. What the timing decides is the *sign* of that alteration relative to the ringing already present.

question: A constant force is switched on at t = 0 and never changed again. The oscillator has Q = 10 and starts at rest. Describe the displacement afterwards.

answers.answer: It overshoots the new equilibrium by about 85% and rings at omega_d before settling at F0/k.
answers.feedback: Right, and this is the module's central surprise. The force has exactly one feature in its whole history, and the response has dozens. The system answers with its own frequency whatever it is asked, and the overshoot exp(-pi gamma / 2 omega_d) depends only on Q — 85% at Q = 10, 44% at Q = 2, zero at critical damping.

answers.answer: It glides smoothly up to F0/k without ever passing it, because the force never decreases.
answers.feedback: This is the misconception the module exists to break: a linear system's displacement does not follow the shape of the force applied to it. Monotonic approach is what happens at critical damping or heavier; at Q = 10 the mass arrives with a velocity it has to lose, and losing it takes 2/gamma of ringing.

answers.answer: It rises to F0/k and stays there immediately, since a constant force has a constant response.
answers.feedback: F0/k is where it *ends*, and that is the steady-state answer to a zero-frequency drive. Getting there is a transient, and the transient is the whole content of this question. The mass has inertia, so it cannot acquire its new position instantly.

answers.answer: It oscillates forever around F0/k, since the force keeps supplying energy.
answers.feedback: A constant force supplies no net energy once the mass has stopped moving, and the damper removes what is there. The ringing decays as e^(-gamma t/2) exactly as a ringdown does — it *is* a ringdown, about the shifted equilibrium.

question: You record a single ringdown of an unknown resonator and take the magnitude of its Fourier transform. What have you got?

answers.answer: The resonator's frequency-response magnitude — module 02's entire swept resonance curve, from one strike.
answers.feedback: Right, and it is the reason engineers test structures with a hammer rather than a shaker. The transform of the impulse response is the frequency response, and one kick contains every frequency at once, so a single record carries the amplitude and phase the sweep would have measured point by point.

answers.answer: The spectrum of the hammer blow, since that is what put the energy in.
answers.feedback: The spectra multiply — x-hat = G-hat F-hat — so what you see is the product. An ideal kick has a flat spectrum, which is exactly why it is the useful probe: it divides out, leaving the resonator's own response and nothing of the hammer's.

answers.answer: A single sharp line at omega_d, because the ringdown is a decaying sinusoid at that frequency.
answers.feedback: A line of zero width would need a sinusoid lasting forever. The decay is what gives the line its width — gamma, full width at half maximum — and that width is precisely the information you want, since Q = omega0/gamma. A decay in time is a Lorentzian in frequency.

answers.answer: Nothing useful without also recording the force, since a transfer function needs an input and an output.
answers.feedback: True in general, and that is why the impulse is special: its transform is a known constant, so the output alone determines the transfer function up to that constant. It is the one input you do not have to measure.

question: Which of these observations would be forbidden by causality alone, given that the system is linear and time-invariant?

answers.answer: The mass has already begun moving one second before the force is first applied.
answers.feedback: Right. Causality is exactly the statement G(t) = 0 for t < 0, which puts the upper limit t on the convolution integral and makes x(t) depend only on the force at times up to t. Motion before the force is the one thing on this list that no choice of m, b, k could produce.

answers.answer: The mass is still moving ten seconds after the force has been switched off.
answers.feedback: Perfectly allowed, and characteristic: the response outlives the force by about 2/gamma. Memory of the past is not a violation of causality — dependence on the future is. This is the ringdown, and it is where you measure Q.

answers.answer: The displacement is largest at a moment when the applied force is zero.
answers.feedback: Allowed and routine. At resonance the displacement lags the force by a quarter cycle, so the peak displacement lands exactly where the force passes through zero. Nothing about that involves the future of the force.

answers.answer: A brief force produces a motion lasting a thousand times longer than the force itself.
answers.feedback: This is the impulse response itself, and it is the module's opening observation: the kick lasts milliseconds and the bell rings for seconds. Causality restricts which direction in time the influence runs, not how long it lasts.

question: A series RLC circuit has L = 10 mH, R = 2.0 ohm and C = 1.0 microfarad. Using the dictionary m <-> L, b <-> R, k <-> 1/C, what is the quality factor Q of this circuit?

answers.feedback: Q = sqrt(L/C)/R = sqrt(0.010 / 1.0e-6) / 2.0 = sqrt(10000) / 2.0 = 100/2.0 = 50. The same arithmetic as sqrt(mk)/b for the mechanical oscillator, because it is the same equation with the symbols renamed. The resonant frequency is omega0 = 1/sqrt(LC) = 10^4 rad/s, about 1.6 kHz.
